Gold Fell 23% From Its Record. What Happened?

2026-11-16

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

COMEX gold futures closed at a record $5,318.40 an ounce on January 29, 2026. By November 6 they were at $4,074.90: down 23%. The worst day came on January 30, when gold fell 10.8% (silver 31%) as Kevin Warsh was named as the pick for Fed chair and the dollar rose. Since then, higher real interest rates, a stronger dollar and the Fed's first rate hike since 2023 pushed gold to a low of $3,898.90 on October 30 (-27%), while central banks kept buying: 321 tonnes in Q3, up 42%. We also look at gold vs stocks, the 2011-2015 gold bust, America's gold at Fort Knox, and whether gold is still a safe haven. 0:00 Intro: gold fell 23% 0:27 What is the gold price? 1:19 The rocket ride 1:52 Why gold soared 2:27 The crash day 3:13 The slow slide 4:16 This has happened before 4:43 Who's still buying 5:37 Gold vs stocks 6:04 Is gold still a safe haven? 6:40 What could turn it around? 7:02 What it means for you 7:29 Recap Sources: Yahoo Finance daily closes for COMEX gold futures (GC=F), silver futures (SI=F) and the S&P 500 (^GSPC), saved Nov 8, 2026; GC=F monthly closes for 2008-2021. Gold just fell 23 percent from its all-time high. On January 29, gold futures closed at a record 5,318 dollars an ounce. On November 6, they closed at 4,075. So what happened? And is gold still the safe haven everyone says it is? Let's look at the data. In the next few minutes: why gold soared, the day it crashed, who is still buying, and whether gold is still a safe haven. First, what are we measuring? Gold is priced per troy ounce, about 31 grams. The price on the news usually comes from gold futures traded in New York, on the COMEX exchange. Gold doesn't pay interest or dividends. Its price comes from who wants it: jewelry makers, investors, central banks, and even tech companies. In the third quarter, electronics alone used 72 tonnes of gold, helped by AI-related manufacturing, according to the World Gold Council. Here's a fun one. The U.S. government owns about 261 million ounces of gold, more than half of it, about 147 million ounces, in Fort Knox, Kentucky. On the government's books, it's still valued at just 42 dollars and 22 cents an ounce: about 11 billion dollars. At the November 6 price, it's worth about 1.07 trillion dollars. First, some perspective. In November 2016, an ounce of gold cost about 1,273 dollars. Even after the drop, it's more than three times that. Gold first closed above 2,000 dollars in August 2020. Above 3,000 in March 2025. Above 4,000 that October. And above 5,000 in January 2026. In 2025 alone, gold gained about 64 percent, its best year in data going back to 2000, with 55 record closes along the way. Why? Analysts point to a few big forces. Force one: central banks. Countries have been buying gold for their reserves, to diversify away from other assets. Force two: interest rates. The Fed cut rates 3 times in 2025. Gold pays no interest, so when rates fall, holding gold costs you less in missed interest. Force three: a weaker dollar. Gold is priced in dollars, and in 2025 the dollar fell about 7.5 percent against a broad basket of currencies. Add worries about wars, tariffs and inflation, and by January, gold was in a frenzy. Then came January 30. That day, President Trump named Kevin Warsh as his pick to lead the Federal Reserve. The dollar rose, and gold futures fell 10.8 percent in a single day. It was gold's worst day in our ten years of data. Many analysts said the run-up had become speculative, and the news was simply the trigger. Silver had it even worse. Silver futures fell 31 percent that same day, and today silver is about 55 percent below its record. Part of the reason is how futures work. One COMEX gold contract is 100 ounces: about 532 thousand dollars of gold at the record. But traders only put down a fraction of that. When prices fall fast, many are forced to sell, and that pushes prices down even faster. Gold bounced back for a while. But since then, three things have kept pushing it down. One: real interest rates. That's what safe government bonds pay after inflation. On January 29, the ten-year real yield was 1.89 percent. Now it's about 2.6. When safe bonds pay more than inflation, gold, which pays nothing, looks less attractive. Ten thousand dollars in inflation-protected Treasury bonds would earn about 260 dollars a year above inflation. Ten thousand dollars of gold earns nothing; it only pays if the price goes up. Two: the dollar got stronger. Since the record, the broad dollar index is up about 3.6 percent. Three: the Fed. In March, it held rates steady, and gold fell almost 6 percent the next day. In September, it raised rates for the first time since 2023, fighting inflation that had climbed back to about 4 percent, partly because of the oil shock after the war with Iran. By October 30, gold was down about 27 percent from its record. Has this happened before? Yes. In August 2011, gold's monthly close hit about 1,828 dollars. Over the next four years, it fell 42 percent, to about 1,060 dollars in December 2015. It took until July 2020, almost nine years after that peak, for gold to get back to its 2011 high. That doesn't mean it will happen again. But it shows how long a gold slump can last. But here's the twist. Not everyone stopped buying. In the third quarter, central banks added 321 tonnes of gold, up 42 percent from a year earlier, according to the World Gold Council. So far this year, they've bought 675 tonnes, 6 percent more than last year. Gold funds took in 211 tonnes, and their total holdings hit a record 4,256 tonnes. These funds let regular investors own gold without storing a single bar. So who stopped? Regular buyers. Jewelry demand fell 17 percent, the weakest third quarter in the council's data. Gold bars and coins fell 19 percent, with China the one big exception, up 7 percent. Even after the drop, gold averaged 4,262 dollars an ounce in the third quarter. For most people, that's still very expensive. And mines dug up a record 1,071 tonnes for a third quarter. How does that compare with stocks? Since January 29, the S&P 500 is up about 6 percent. Over the last twelve months, about 10 percent. Over ten years, both roughly tripled. Gold, about 3.2 times. The S&P 500, about 3.5 times, counting prices only. That's about 12 percent a year for gold, and 13 for stocks. And stocks paid dividends on top. Gold never pays anything while you hold it. So is gold still a safe haven? It depends what you mean. Over ten years, gold has more than tripled. Over the last twelve months, it's up only about 2 percent. And since January, it's down almost a quarter. Anyone who bought one ounce at the record is down about 1,243 dollars. Gold's big strength is that it isn't anyone's debt: no company or government has to pay it back, and it can help when the dollar falls. But it can swing wildly, and it pays no interest or dividends. And with inflation at about 4 percent, that 2 percent gain over a year actually lost value. So what could turn gold around? Nobody knows, and we don't make predictions. But the same forces that pushed it down can work in reverse. If real interest rates fall, if the dollar weakens, or if the Fed starts cutting again, gold could get support. And central banks are still buying. And if rates and the dollar keep rising, the pressure could continue. We don't give financial advice, but the data teaches three lessons. One: a safe haven doesn't mean a safe price. Gold fell almost 11 percent in one day, and silver 31. Two: watch real interest rates and the dollar. This year, when they went up, gold went down. Three: when something rises 64 percent in a year, the ride down can be fast too. And after 2011, the wait to get back took almost nine years. If you own gold, know why you own it. Let's recap. Gold hit a record 5,318 dollars in January, then fell 23 percent. The crash day came with a new pick for Fed chair. Since then, higher real rates, a stronger dollar and a Fed hike pushed it lower, while central banks kept buying.
